content: 1. The risk of bias was downgraded by two levels due to unclear or high risk of bias across all studies. This included issues related to random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants, blinding of care providers, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, baseline group similarity, co-interventions, and compliance with the intervention. 2. Inconsistency was downgraded by one level due to unexplained substantial heterogeneity, with an I² value of 71%. 3. Imprecision was downgraded by two levels due to wide confidence intervals that were consistent with both the possibility of benefit and the possibility of no effect, as well as a low number of participants. 4. The risk of bias was downgraded by two levels in another set of studies due to similar issues, including unclear or high risk of bias in random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants, blinding of care providers, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and compliance with the intervention. 5. Inconsistency was downgraded by one level due to unexplained considerable heterogeneity, with an I² value of 87%. 6. In another analysis, inconsistency was downgraded by one level due to unexplained substantial heterogeneity, with an I² value of 86%. 7. In cases where only one study was included in the analysis, inconsistency was not assessed. 8. Indirectness was downgraded by one level in a subgroup analysis because only one study was included, and it was unclear if the findings were representative of all high-income countries. 9. Imprecision was downgraded by two levels in some studies due to wide confidence intervals consistent with the possibility of harm and the possibility of no effect, as well as a low number of participants. 10. Imprecision was downgraded by two levels in another analysis because no events were reported in either group. 11. The follow-up time for some studies was reported as 3–12 weeks, while for others, it was 20 weeks or 6 weeks. 12. Therapeutic ultrasound was evaluated for its benefits and harms in managing chronic primary low back pain in community-dwelling adults, including older adults aged 60 years and over, compared to usual care. 13. Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) was defined as a non-invasive peripheral electrical stimulation modality applied to the skin using surface electrodes. It uses low-voltage electrical currents to modify the perception of pain through segmental inhibition or activation of descending nociceptive-inhibitory systems. 14. TENS devices can be used in healthcare facilities or as portable devices for home use. Various stimulation parameters, such as pulse intensity, frequency, duration, and type (burst or continuous), can be selected based on clinical indications. 15. In the included trials, TENS interventions involved electrode placement over the paravertebral lumbosacral area and sometimes the affected leg in cases of associated leg pain, using conventional continuous or burst pulse parameters. 16. Critical outcomes for evaluating interventions included pain, back-specific function/disability, general function/disability, health-related quality of life, psychosocial function, social participation, adverse events, changes in medication use, and falls. 17. No evidence synthesis was commissioned for all adults or older adults regarding values and preferences, resource considerations, acceptability, or feasibility. Judgments were based on the experience of guideline development group (GDG) members. 18. Trials on depression stratified by gender, race/ethnicity, number of treatment sessions, national economic development, or presence of leg pain were not identified. Similarly, trials on fear avoidance, catastrophizing, anxiety, or self-efficacy were not identified. 19. No TENS-associated adverse events were reported in any participants in the included trials. 20. The GRADE framework was used to assess the quality of evidence, with specific criteria for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and other considerations such as publication bias. 21. Four trials included multiple arms comparing different TENS modalities (e.g., high-frequency TENS, low-frequency TENS, burst TENS) versus sham interventions.
